Digital Voices update: a new voice for Alexander

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Following our digital voices story earlier this year, Alexander Avenant has received the first South African child's voice.

Unique Selling Point:
A story that shows the power of positive change that can come with a little exposure. After watching Carte Blanche's digital voices story earlier this year, three Pretoria schoolboys have donated their voices to allow our case study Alexander to speak with the voice of the child he is.

Summary:
Three Pretoria schoolboys watched our story about Alternative and Augmentative Communication devices for those who cannot speak with their own voices. Inspired by the story of Alexander who was able to speak with an Afrikaans AAC voice, but had to use a man's voice, the boys decided to donate their own voices. They approached the CSIR and one of the boys was selected. he then spent multiple days during his holiday in the CSIR recording studio and the result was "Bennie", the first Qfrency child's voice and therefore the first child's voice available in a local South African language. Alexander is delighted with his new voice, which is now available off the shelf for other children. Meanwhile, some local school girls have also got on board and are now donating their voices too.

Press Release:


Just because you can't speak, doesn't mean you have nothing to say. In May this year, Carte Blanche met Alexander Avenant, who cannot speak due to brain injury, and used a synthetic man's voice to communicate. Inspired by our story, three Pretoria schoolboys have donated their voices to allow Alexander to speak with the voice of the child he is.

Script:


VO1: Just because you can’t speak, doesn’t mean you have nothing to say. Alexander Avenant will never develop speech as a result of brain damage sustained as a baby. He relies on software to convert onscreen text to synthetic speech.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Hoe het jy gevoel toe jy dit vir die eerste keer gebruik het en Afrikaans kon praat?
Alexander Avenant: Ek was baie opgewonde.
Stephanie: Was iets vir jou snaaks gewees?
Alexander: Die oom stem het my baie laat lag.
VO2: Alexander communicates in his home language thanks to Qfrency, synthesised voices for all 11 official South African languages. But when we met him in May this year, this little boy spoke with the deep voice of a grown man.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Dink jy wanner jou maatjies die stem hoor, hoor hulle jou?
Alexander Avenant: Nee, hulle hoor die oom se stem.
UPSOUND: Stephanie Stander: Hierdie man stem wat hierdie eenvoudige werkies antwoord is – dis ‘n vreemde vreemde ding om te hoor.
VO3: Stephanie Stander is Alexander’s Grade 1 teacher at Nuwe Hoop Skool in Pretoria.
UPSOUND: Stephanie Stander: Dit maak net meer sin vir ‘n kind om met ‘n kind stem te praat. Omdat hulle nog speel en storietjies vertel.
UPSOUND: Karen Calteaux The only voices that are available in South Africa for our local languages and our local English accent are adult voices.
VO4: Dr Karen Calteaux and her speech technology team at the Meraka Institute developed the Qfrency voices.
UPSOUND: Dr Karen Calteaux: We’ve tried in the past to do a child’s voice, but it’s very hard because the recording protocol is quite strict. So we usually use professional voice artists.
VO5: Inspired by our story, Gerard Jordaan, Chris Engelbrecht and Johan Nel from Constantia Park Primary set out to change that by donating their voices to Alexander.
UPSOUND: Gerard Jordaan: Ek het gedink dat dit nie reg is dat Alexander met ‘n oom stem praat nie en ek het geweet ons moet iets vir hom doen. Want ons het die vermoë om dit te doen.
UPSOUND: Chris Engelbrecht: Dis ‘n ongelooflike ding wat jy kan vir ‘n mens doen om ‘n stem te gee.
UPSOUND: Karen Calteaux: It’s extremely exciting but it’s also a bit scary.
VO6: In the internet age, says Calteaux, donating your voice should not be taken lightly.
UPSOUND: Karen Calteaux: Once a voice has been built using a child’s recordings, that voice can be used by anybody to say anything. But when we were approached by these children and they were so excited to actually do this, we thought well let’s give it a go.
VO7: Fuelled by the boys’ enthusiasm, the process began with voice auditions.
UPSOUND: Dr Karen Calteaux: It’s very important that they must read fluently. It’s important that their accent needs to be as standard as possible. It’s important that they don’t switch between languages and that they sound like a first language speaker. We had to make sure of course that the children – that their voices hadn’t broken yet otherwise they wouldn’t sound like boys.
UPSOUND: Johan Nel: Hulle wou die jongste as moontlik stem vir Alexander hê en uit ons drie was dit ek.
VO8: Johan spent his June holiday reading text selected to cover every sound combination in the Afrikaans language.
UPSOUND: Dr Karen Calteaux: You’re required to read about 3000 prompts, sentences in a recording studio over a period of about 5 days at 6 hours a day.
UPSOUND: Johan Nel: Na ‘n rukkie word jy gewoond daaraan. Dis die – dis maar net praat, kan nie so moeg wees nie.
UPSOUND: Stephanie Stander: Ek kon dit eintlik nie glo dat sulke jong outjies bereid is om so baie tyd van hulleself op te gee om dit te doen vir ‘n kind nie.
VO9: A week’s recording produced a small audio sample – but enough data for Karen’s team to model and build Bennie, the first synthetic South African child’s voice.
UPSOUND: Dr Karen Calteaux: We were a bit sceptical initially, we didn’t think we’d get the quality that we got. So we are absolutely ecstatic.
UPSOUND: Gerhard Jordaan: Ek was baie opgewonde want ek het gesien hoe my, of hoe ons die idee gerealiseer het.
UPSOUND: Stephanie Stander: Ek het sommer begin huil toe ek dit vir die eerste keer hoor.
VO10: For Alexander, his new voice came as a big surprise.
UPSOUND: Stephanie Stander: Is julle opgewonde om te hoor hoe Alexander van nou af gaan klink? Is julle opgewonde?
Alexander Avenant: Ek will graag dankie sê.
Stephanie Stander: Dis jou nuwe stem!
UPSOUND: Stephanie Stander: Alexie, laas keer het jy gesê jy hou van die oom stem. Maar hour jy meer van die Bennie stem?
Alexander Avenant: Ja baie. Dis lekkerder ook om my tablet te gebruik.
Stephanie Stander: Hoekom is die Bennie stem beter as die oom stem?
Alexander Avenant: Ek klink nou soos my maatjies in die klas.
UPSOUND: Stephanie Stander: Die maatjies in die klas is gewoond aan hierdie man stem wat gepraat het. En eweskielik kan hulle ook meer vereenselwig met Alexander want hy is ook nou eweskielik soos ‘n seuntjie soos hulle.
UPSOUND: Stephanie Stander: Voel jy asof jou maats jou anders behandel met die nuwe stem?
Alexander Avenant: Ja. Hulle sê self hul hour meer van die nuwe stem.
VO11: And in just a few weeks, the impact on Alexander has been remarkable.
UPSOUND: Stephanie Stander: Hy’s baie meer positief om op sy tablet te werk. Hy was aanvanklik nie lus nie en sou eerder self met sy hande vir ons verbaliseer. Maar nou is hy opgewonde om sy tablet te gebruik en hy wil alles doen en saam gesels.
UPSOUND: Chris Engelbrecht: Ek dink dis baie belangrik dat hy kommunikeer met die regte stem soos Johan se stem met ‘n kind se stem wat vir hom die geleentheid gee om boog te kommunikeer.
UPSOUND: Gerard Jordaan: Dit sal dalk net ‘n bietjie meer normal voel en sy maats sal dalk net ‘n bietjie meer gemaklik met hom praat.
VO12: Bennie is now available for purchase, and Calteaux says they are hoping to keep expanding the Qfrency range.
UPSOUND: Dr Karen Calteaux: we all have our own unique personal voice. And if you think about it, that’s what you want to be able to provide to people who don’t have their own voice.
VO13: And what does Johan think of his voice being preserved for the ages?
UPSOUND: Johan Nel: Ten minste dat ek onthou sal word lank daarna ek weg is.

PROMO 1: 10 SECONDS
VO: In May, Carte Blanche met Alexander Avenant, a little boy who spoke with a synthetic man’s voice. Now three school-boys have given him a voice for himself.

PROMO 2: 15 SECONDS
VO: When we first met Alexander Avenant, his digital voice sounded like a grown man. But now thanks to three school-boys, he sounds like the child he is.
Stephanie Stander: Hoekom is die Bennie stem beter as die oom stem?
Alexander Avenant: Ek klink nou soos my maatjies in die klas.

PROMO 3: 15 SECONDS
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Dink jy wanner jou maatjies die stem hoor, hoor hulle jou?
Alexander Avenant: Nee, hulle hoor die oom se stem.
VO: When we first met Alexander Avenant, his digital voice sounded like a grown man. But now three school-boys have gifted him with a new voice.

PROMO 4: 30 SECONDS
VO: Just because you can’t speak, doesn’t mean you have nothing to say. But synthetic voices don’t always suit their owners.
UPSOUND: Stephanie Stander: Hierdie man stem wat hierdie eenvoudige werkies antwoord is – dis ‘n vreemde vreemde ding om te hoor.
VO: When we first met Alexander Avenant, his digital voice had the deep tones of a grown man. But now thanks to a donation from three schoolboys, he sounds like the child he is.
UPSOUND: Chris Engelbrecht: Dis ‘n ongelooflike ding wat jy kan vir ‘n mens doen om ‘n stem te gee.
